newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil steps up fight to tame external accounts.
newsitem.headline: Brazil steps up fight to tame external accounts.

text.p: Brazil's decision to hold monthly interest rates steady in May ends an eight-month pattern of rate cuts and confirms growing official concern over a burgeoning current account gap, economists said.
The move to leave the Central Bank's basic interest rate (TBC) unchanged from April's 1.58 percent surprised the market, which had grown accostomed to steady rate cuts.

Analysts welcomed the move but said further measures would be needed to tame Brazil's current account gap, which is expected to top $30 billion this year, or about 4.0 percent of gross domestic product.

"This is a positive and prudent measure to have more control over the current account deficit," said Marcelo Audi, chief economist at Merrill Lynch in Brazil. "It is also in line with expectations that the government, maybe in the short term, could adopt more restrictive credit measures."
The decision to leave rates unchanged was widely viewed as the second step by the government this year to slow deterioration of Brazil's external accounts.
The first move came in late March when the Central Bank slapped restrictions on short-term import financing to slow a trade gap that is forecast to hit about $10 billion in 1997.
Economists said Wednesday's move, however, was aimed less at trade accounts and more at maintaining foreign reserves at current levels of about $58 billion.
"This has more to do with capital flows than import controls," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist at ING Bank in Brazil.
During the first three months of this year, Brazil's foreign reserves fell by about $1.0 billion, indicating there were insufficient funds to finance the current account deficit.
Economists said policy-makers are concerned Brazil will not attract enough capital to finance its current account gap if interest rates fall too low.

"I think the Central Bank wanted to send the market a signal that it would not allow the exchange coupon (the spread differential in interest rates and exchange rate depreciation) to fall much further," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at Banco BMC in Brazil.
The exchange coupon, effectively the rate of return for foreign investors in Brazilian fixed-income securities, has fallen to about 10 percent from above 20 percent at the end of 1995, Allain said.

Economists said last month's hike in U.S. interest rates and expectations for further increases by the Federal Reserve Board did not figure prominently in the Central Bank's decision to leave rates unchanged. Brazilian interest rate policy, they said, is largely independent of U.S. policy.

After restricting import financing and stablizing interest rates, Brasilia was next expected to adopt credit restrictions on consumer consumption to bolster its fight against import growth. And many economists expect those new restrictions to come sooner than later.
"Wednesday's interest rate move in no way diminishes the chance of credit restrictions on consumer consumption in the future," ING's Schneider said.
